These declarations allow the reader and writer classes to access private members of the value_type class. Reader class directly accesses and modifies mimeFields and Writer class access file related members to read data from file

We're now at the point where we have 3 embedded types here.  Checking fileHandle.is_open() was a relatively easy way to tell which was being used for any given body.  Now that we have a third, I suspect this needs to become a std::variant<std::string, DuplicatableFileHandle, std::vector<FormPart>>;
This might need some rework and would increase the scope of this patch. Shall we take this up as a follow up commit ?
Feel free to put it as a patch ahead of this if you're worried about this patch getting to large, but I don't like the subtlety that this can be one of three different types.
Sure, I'll be creating a patch for this.
I see the patch.  Would like to see the variant done first so this patchset is reviewable.  If that's not something you can manage, I can do it.
@ed@tanous.net I've made this change, kindly re-review the patch.
The code is broken after this change, let me fix it first. Will update here once done.
Sounds good.  Thank you.
I've merged the variant patch in this one. As it was mostly refactoring the code from this patch.

Another thing to consider here is that now all URIs will now implicitly support reading multipart requests.  We should make some attempt to disallow that in the obvious cases.

Checking the verb is POST before allowing multipart would be a good start, and would remove a lot of the obvious footguns that would give a weird error message back to the user.
I've added a check for POST method. Please review.

Please fix this check.

1. !multipartParser will always be true when this is called after construction
2. We have content-type parsers now.  Please use them.
3. !contentType.empty() is redundant if the next check is comparing starts_with
Acknowledged
No need to reset it here.  We're returning an error, the whole reader object is about to be destroyed.
Makes sense, I'll revert this
Done

Keep in mind, when we hit parsing errors, we need to be able to return 400 bad request from the handler.  As written, I suspect you want to just set an internal error, that the handler can read back on multipart().

Just revisited the http_connection code — shouldn't this be handled in afterRead()? We could add a condition to specifically check for bad_message there.

From what I understand of the current design, the execution will never reach the update_service handler because afterRead() calls gracefulClose() as soon as any error is encountered.

Please correct me if I’m missing something.

> Just revisited the http_connection code — shouldn't this be handled in afterRead()? We could add a condition to specifically check for bad_message there.

the connection class isn't in charge of responses, the router is.  Hardcoding this in http connection would mean that we'd have to hardcode one specific error return, rather than a per-uri error return.

Redfish should respond with a redfish json payload 400 error
Login routes should respond with their specific 400 error code.

> 
> From what I understand of the current design, the execution will never reach the update_service handler because afterRead() calls gracefulClose() as soon as any error is encountered.

Right....  this isn't an "error" in the normal sense.  For files and strings the only kind of errors are internal errors the user can do nothing about (ie 500 errors).

This flow should return a 400 error, that the user could do something about by correcting their response, so the body needs to basically mark that the parse failed, and return that when the specific handler requests the mime data.

The "right" solution would be what we did for 401, which would be to add yet another condition to the routing table, and register a redfish-specific "400" handler.  I don't want to make you do that work for what's ultimately one URI.

> 
> Please correct me if I’m missing something.
I've handled this in the code, please re-review.
Roll this into the above branch.  there's no case where multipartParser gets set without the above branch running.
Agree, I'll make the change.
Done
We already have TemporaryFileHandle that fulfills basically this same use case, although might be missing a couple mesthods (that can be added).  Any reason we avoided that?

For multipart uploads we additionally need to - 
1. create a secure temp file (mkstemp)
2. remember the path so we can rename()/copy it to /tmp/images/<uuid>
3. auto-unlink the temp file on every failure path.

These behaviours would change the lifetime rules of the existing class, e.g. a copied handle would suddenly have to agree on who deletes the file, so I've added a separate TemporaryReleasableFileHandle to keep the original semantics of DuplicatableFileHandle untouched.

Test Results and performance charts for different scenarios are captured in this doc- https://docs.google.com/document/d/1EXFMc9tLzQsfyYtF6nuAVw6yadIjUQkwnalU34Vl4uU/edit?pli=1&tab=t.0#heading=h.ax2n0js5wlay
Initial round of comments
This is one of the parts that should mark the failure in the response somehow.
Acknowledged
This API needs to give some indication to the caller when multipart parsing failed.

The API has been updated to return std::optional<std::vector<FormPart>>

Success case: Returns a valid optional containing the parsed FormPart vector
Failure case: Returns std::nullopt when multipart parsing fails
This looks like we're completely removing support for multipart form logins?  i'm assuming that's not intentional?
Reverted this change
This looks like it will fail if we've converted content to a file.
Fixed by adding type-safe content access. Instead of always calling contentString(), we now check the content variant type first
This is a header, static isn't correct, inline might be correct.
As part of rework, this code is removed.
?  How were these conditions chosen?  These look like they're hardcoding redfish specifics (ie UpdateFile).
Removed Redfish-specific hardcoding. Now using only the standard HTTP filename= parameter in Content-Disposition header to detect file uploads.

Why are we doing this in the finish() call?  Shouldn't this be done incrementally as parsing is completed?  Otherwise this is no more efficient than what we had (we still have to read the whole request into ram).

Originally planned to buffer up to 1MB in RAM before writing to file (to reduce IO operations), to handle cases where image is less than 1MB, I added this logic in finish().
But I've removed this approach in the rework- we are writing the subsequent chunks directly to file now
We have several file classes already with various levels of "goodness".  Please reuse one of the existing and add your logic to it.  DuplicatableFileHandle or TemporaryFileHandle might be similar?
Refractored the code to extend the existing DuplicatableFileHandle class
should we make this just /tmp ?  we already have a bmcweb prefix.

In our bmc paltforms, /tmp/ and /tmp/images are on different filesystem.

On cross file system, a copy is required which means 2x memory usage
But on same filesystem -> rename() succeeds → No extra copy

I've captured the free memory graph for different scenarios here- https://docs.google.com/document/d/1EXFMc9tLzQsfyYtF6nuAVw6yadIjUQkwnalU34Vl4uU/edit?pli=1&tab=t.0#heading=h.ax2n0js5wlay. Please take a look

> In our bmc paltforms, /tmp/ and /tmp/images are on different filesystem.

Lets just do /tmp/bmcweb/<file>

Then on your platforms you're free to symlink that directory wherever you like.

> On cross file system, a copy is required which means 2x memory usage

I don't understand this.  if it's cross filesystem, you're not using memory, you're using filesystem.

On different filesystems, a move() operation will not be an atomic metadata operation, it becomes copy + delete operation.

So both the files will exist simulataneously during the copy and therefore free memory drops by 2X.

| Lets just do /tmp/bmcweb/<file> 
-> how about using a meson build option, I can set the default to /tmp/bmcweb/<file> ?
Lets focus on what openbmc does, which doesn't currently have the problem you've described.  You are free to do whatever you like in your downstream, or propose a new filesystem format upstream.
Acknowledged
